opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because on the surface they sound contradictory. But in practice they're two sides of the same thing.

Most of the work is careful prioritization. You have limited compute, limited people, and way more ideas than you could ever run. So you spend a lot of time asking: what's the cheapest experiment that would change my mind? You start small, run ablations, look at the data really closely, read a lot of model outputs, and build intuition about whether something is actually working or just looks good on one eval. That discipline is what earns you the right to take bigger bets.

The YOLO run comes in when you've accumulated enough signal that you believe in a direction, but the small-scale experiments can't fully tell you whether it'll pay off. Some behaviors only show up at scale, or only when you combine several changes at once. If you insist on de-risking every single component independently, you can spend months and still not know. At some point you have to say: I have a strong hypothesis, the downside is bounded, and the upside is big enough. Let's just try it.

So for me, the reconciliation is something like: be rigorous about what goes *into* the YOLO run, and be honest about what you'll learn *from* it. Before kicking it off, I want to know what success looks like, what failure looks like, and what I'd do in each case. Even if it fails, it should fail informatively. If it fails and you can't tell why, that's the bad kind of YOLO.

And taste plays a huge role. A lot of research is knowing which corners you can cut and which ones you absolutely can't. Data quality, for example, is usually not a corner you want to cut. Whereas trying an exhaustive hyperparameter sweep before you even know the idea has legs? Often you can skip that.

The other thing I'd say is that the culture matters. If people get punished for a failed bold run, nobody takes bold bets, and you end up with very incremental progress. But if YOLO runs are just "let's see what happens" with no thought behind them, you burn a lot of compute. The sweet spot is a team where people are encouraged to take big swings, but those swings come from deep intuition built through lots of careful small experiments.

r001.rationale: It says compute is limited and that researchers should use small experiments before taking bigger YOLO bets, identifying compute availability as a constraint on those runs.

r002.rationale: It describes building conviction through small experiments and intuition, but does not identify rapidly building conviction as a central task of research management.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think they're actually in tension, honestly. The YOLO run and the carefully prioritized experiment are answering different questions, and the skill is knowing which question you're asking.

When we were building out the first versions of Claude's writing and conversational style, a lot of the early work was tiny, cheap, almost embarrassingly small experiments. Change one thing in the data, train a small model, look at the samples with your own eyes. You're trying to build intuition about which direction the gradient points, so to speak. Those experiments are prioritized ruthlessly because they're cheap and you can run many of them, and each one should kill or confirm a hypothesis. If an experiment doesn't change what you'd do next, it's not worth running.

The YOLO run is a different animal. It's expensive, it's slow, and it's the moment where you commit to a bet. But a good YOLO run isn't actually reckless. It's the culmination of all those small experiments. You've de-risked the individual pieces, you have a thesis about how they compose, and you just can't learn the last thing without putting it all together at scale. Some behaviors only show up at scale. Some data mixtures interact in ways you can't predict from ablations. So you have to go.

Where people get it wrong is doing YOLO runs on things that could have been tested cheaply, or doing endless small experiments on something that will only ever be resolved by the big run. Both are forms of avoiding the real decision.

The other thing I'd say is that taste matters a lot here. Part of why you can take the big swing is that you've looked at thousands of samples and you have a feel for what's going to work. That's not a replacement for rigor, but it's what tells you which of the hundred possible big bets is the one worth making. The careful prioritization earns you the right to YOLO.

astra-6.text:
I think those are complementary. You want to be very deliberate about the question you’re asking, but you don’t need to know the answer before you run the experiment. Otherwise, you’re probably not taking enough risk.

For me, prioritization is about asking: If this works, how much does it change what we can do? And if it doesn’t, will we learn something that changes our next decision? A YOLO run can be valuable when it tests an intuition that smaller experiments can’t really resolve. But you still want a clear hypothesis and some idea of what you’ll do with the result.

So I’d keep most of the work focused on experiments with a strong rationale, while leaving room for a few bets that are harder to justify upfront. The important thing is to update afterward—to avoid becoming attached to an idea just because you took a big swing on it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are complementary. You want to be thoughtful about which questions are worth spending compute on, but you don’t want to require certainty before you try something. Otherwise, you end up doing only incremental experiments.

For me, the important thing is having a hypothesis: What do we think might happen, and what would we learn if we’re wrong? You can prioritize that carefully and still take a chance on a run where your intuition says there’s something interesting. “YOLO” shouldn’t mean there’s no reasoning behind it. It means you’re willing to act before you have all the evidence.
